stories.title: What is the best harness for each model?
stories.author: Edward40

topComments.author: guanlan
topComments.text: Hi HN, I’m Guanlan, founder of Runta. The eval runs on our runtime, so weigh this accordingly. The short version: when you change the model, think about changing the harness too. On any one model, cost per pass varies by up to 4.4x What we ran: 22 harness configurations × 5 open-weight models × 62 terminal tasks × 4 attempts. 27,280 runs, 83B tokens. Each harness ran with default settings at maximum reasoning effort, each trial in a fresh sandbox. Costs are Baseten list prices times reported tokens. What we found: The lowest-cost harness changes with the model. Codex CLI ranks 1st on cost with GLM-5.3 and 15th with Kimi-K3. Paying more doesn’t buy passes. The harness with the highest pass rate ranked anywhere from 4th to 19th on cost. The model still sets most of the bill (93% of cost variation). The harness is the second lever. Starting prompt size doesn’t predict cost. Output tokens do. 64% of inference spend went to runs that didn’t pass.

topComments.author: Majromax
topComments.text: Saying that 'steps per pass' explains cost seems nearly tautological. Run costs are proportional to the number of tokens produced, and the number of tokens is strongly correlated to the number of steps. The 'steps per pass' criterion is also not something under the harness's direct control in the way that its tool collection and system prompt (/start tokens) are. Even the cache hit rate is hard to control beyond a limit, since modern harnesses rarely rewrite history. I'm also suspicious about the run-to-run variance between models. Given the high variability within the presented results and the observation that failed runs (which can spin for a long time before delivering a wrong answer) account for a majority of the cost, I'm not sure that many of the conclusions here would hold up under a second sample.

And yes, I used Claude a lot this year for the grind: stripping out JavaScript, the dark themes, the test suite. Happy to talk about how that went. MIT, about 24 KB gzipped, from jsDelivr or npm. stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I want to write a bit of code that catches all exceptions thrown from a third-party function, takes a look at the exception message, and re-throws the exception later. I have written it like this: std::string message = Foo(); std::exception_ptr eptr = nullptr; try { ThirdPartyMayThrow(); } catch (...) { // (1) eptr = std::current_exception(); try { throw; } catch (const std::exception &e) { (message += ": ") += e.what(); // append what } catch (...) { // (2) } } SendMessage(message); if (eptr) { std::rethrow_exception(eptr); } I want all exceptions from ThirdPartyMayThrow() to be caught before I call SendMessage and re-thrown afterwards if eptr was set. Do I need clause (2) to make sure no exception is still actively propagating when the program gets out of clause (1), or does storing a pointer to the current exception already prevent that? Is there a better way to do this without code duplication?

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Getting Combination Permutations of Several Lists, With Segments of Length N

stackOverflowQuestions.title: SQL semi-join anti-pattern in DB2
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I am often required to optimize SQL statements, and over the years I got to recognize the very same anti-patterns. One of those anti-patterns is as follows: SELECT A.PK_A_1 ,A.PK_A_2 FROM TABLE_PARENTS A WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM TABLE_CHILDREN B WHERE A.PK_A_1 = B.PK_B_1 AND A.PK_A_2 = B.PK_B_2 ) -- BETTER REWRITING SELECT A.PK_A_1 ,A.PK_A_2 FROM TABLE_PARENTS A INNER JOIN ( SELECT PK_B_1 ,PK_B_2 FROM TABLE_CHILDREN GROUP BY PK_B_1 ,PK_B_2 ) B ON A.PK_A_1 = B.PK_B_1 AND A.PK_A_2 = B.PK_B_2 This recipe has always worked great for Oracle 11g / 19c, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Informix, etc. Yet, I found out with great surprise that in DB2 v13 for z/OS the antipattern performs better than the rewriting. Question: Has someone experienced this beahaviour before, and could ellaborate as to why the so-called-anti-pattern performs better? P.D.: The real SQL I am dealing with is much more complex, but, if needed, I could run some mockup INSERTs and populate real tables to acquire execution plans (access paths), volumetries, column cardinalities, index coverages, etc.

I am trying to understand how React handles state updates when the new state is identical to the previous state. Consider the following React component: import { useState, useEffect } from 'react'; export default function App() { const [resource, setResource] = useState("user"); console.log("render"); useEffect(() => { console.log("resource changed"); }); return ( <>

{resource}

); } When I run the application, I observe the following console outputs: Initial render: render resource changed Click the User button (initial state is already "user" ): No output is printed. Click the Posts button (state changes from "user" to "posts" ): render resource changed Click the Posts button again (state is already "posts" ): render Interestingly, clicking the User button when the state is already "user" does not print anything, whereas clicking the Posts button again, when the state is already "posts" , prints "render" but not "resource changed" . According to React documentation, React uses Object.is() to compare the previous state with the new state. If both values are identical, React can skip re-rendering the component. However, in my observation, React sometimes invokes the component function even when the state has not changed. Why does React invoke the component function when Posts is clicked for the second time but not when User is clicked? I would appreciate an explanation of the underlying React rendering mechanism rather than just the general rule that React skips updates when the state remains unchanged.
